scenes.tts: The first film separated a variant's origin from selection. Now a D N A strip is damaged; is the cell mutated yet? Follow how that variant begins. The red mark appears before any daughter sequence has formed.
scenes.caption: The first film separated a variant's origin from selection. Now a DNA strip is damaged; is the cell mutated yet? Follow how that variant begins. The red mark appears before any daughter sequence has formed.
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's 16:9 world and colour map: unchanged DNA BLUE; changed sequence YELLOW; damage or outside agents RED; accurate repair GREEN; neutral labels WHITE. Rewind to the blue ancestor just before the first film's early yellow branch began, then zoom into that cell. Its DNA is a large row of labelled blue blocks, never a molecular structure. A red crack mark lands on one block. Later scenes reconnect the resulting yellow lineage to that branch. The question 'Mutation yet?' appears above it. A small 'schematic' label remains visible throughout.
scenes.narration: The first film separated a variant's origin from selection. Now a DNA strip is damaged; is the cell mutated yet? Follow how that variant begins. The red mark appears before any daughter sequence has formed.

scenes.visual: Title 'When Damage Becomes Mutation' appears for two seconds above the blue block strip. The red damage mark pulses, and a copying conveyor moves slowly beneath it.

scenes.tts: A mutation is a heritable change in D N A sequence. Heritable matters here. A temporary chemical lesion is damage, but it is not automatically a changed sequence. The sequence must change and persist when the cell divides.
scenes.caption: A mutation is a heritable change in DNA sequence. Heritable matters here. A temporary chemical lesion is damage, but it is not automatically a changed sequence. The sequence must change and persist when the cell divides.
scenes.visual: Place two large labels above the carried strip: 'damage' over the RED mark and 'sequence' over the BLUE block order. The red mark flickers while the letters on the blue blocks remain unchanged. A WHITE bracket highlights 'heritable change' and stays empty, showing that the criterion has not yet been met.
scenes.narration: A mutation is a heritable change in DNA sequence. Heritable matters here. A temporary chemical lesion is damage, but it is not automatically a changed sequence. The sequence must change and persist when the cell divides.

scenes.tts: Changes can begin in two broad ways. Copying can place the wrong block. Or chemistry can damage a block before the next copy. Either route can end without a mutation.
scenes.caption: Changes can begin in two broad ways. Copying can place the wrong block. Or chemistry can damage a block before the next copy. Either route can end without a mutation.
scenes.visual: The same block strip travels left to right through a large copying station. On the upper lane, the station places one YELLOW block into a new BLUE strip. On the lower lane, a RED damage badge lands on an existing blue block before that strip reaches the station. The lanes remain side by side and labelled 'copying error' and 'damage'.
scenes.narration: Changes can begin in two broad ways. Copying can place the wrong block. Or chemistry can damage a block before the next copy. Either route can end without a mutation.

scenes.tts: Damage enters a fork. Repair may restore the original block. If repair misses it, copying may preserve the original sequence or produce a different one. The lesion's presence does not choose the outcome.
scenes.caption: Damage enters a fork. Repair may restore the original block. If repair misses it, copying may preserve the original sequence or produce a different one. The lesion's presence does not choose the outcome.
scenes.visual: The damaged lower lane reaches a large Y-shaped junction. One branch leads through a GREEN repair gate back to an all-blue strip. The other passes the red-marked block into the copying station, then splits again toward an all-blue daughter or a daughter containing one yellow block. All outcomes remain visible without a verdict.
scenes.narration: Damage enters a fork. Repair may restore the original block. If repair misses it, copying may preserve the original sequence or produce a different one. The lesion's presence does not choose the outcome.

scenes.tts: Before the strip reaches that fork, predict: must a red damage mark become a mutation? Trace every possible path before choosing.
scenes.caption: Before the strip reaches that fork, predict: must a red damage mark become a mutation? Trace every possible path before choosing.
scenes.visual: Rewind the damaged strip to the entrance of the fork. Show two neutral daughter-strip outlines beyond it. A large question spans the frame: 'Must the damage become a mutation?' The green repair path, blue original path and yellow changed path are dim but visible.
scenes.narration: Before the strip reaches that fork, predict: must a red damage mark become a mutation? Trace every possible path before choosing.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. The damaged strip waits at the fork. The red mark pulses gently, the green gate glows softly, and the daughter outlines drift slightly.

scenes.tts: No. On one path, repair removes the lesion and restores the blue block. After copying, both daughter strips keep the original sequence. The cell had damage, yet no mutation remains.
scenes.caption: No. On one path, repair removes the lesion and restores the blue block. After copying, both daughter strips keep the original sequence. The cell had damage, yet no mutation remains.
scenes.visual: Brighten the GREEN path. The damaged strip enters the repair gate; the red mark lifts away and a blue replacement block slides into place. The restored strip copies. Two all-blue daughter strips emerge, and the empty 'heritable change' bracket stays empty.
scenes.narration: No. On one path, repair removes the lesion and restores the blue block. After copying, both daughter strips keep the original sequence. The cell had damage, yet no mutation remains.

scenes.tts: On another path, copying places a wrong block opposite the lesion. At the next copy, that wrong block templates a full base-pair change. The damaged strand goes to a separate daughter, where repair or bypass can follow. In the changed lineage the lesion is gone, but its consequence persists.
scenes.caption: On another path, copying places a wrong block opposite the lesion. At the next copy, that wrong block templates a full base-pair change. The damaged strand goes to a separate daughter, where repair or bypass can follow. In the changed lineage the lesion is gone, but its consequence persists.
scenes.visual: Rewind to the fork and brighten the copying path. The red-marked block enters the station. A YELLOW wrong block appears opposite the red lesion, so the first copy yields one strip pairing the lesion with a mismatch. On the next copy the strands separate: the yellow wrong-base strand templates one strip with a stable yellow base-pair change, while the red lesion-bearing parental strand moves into a separate dim branch labelled 'repair or bypass'. Only the stable yellow strip continues into descendants. The WHITE 'heritable change' bracket closes around that stable yellow position.
scenes.narration: On another path, copying places a wrong block opposite the lesion. At the next copy, that wrong block templates a full base-pair change. The damaged strand goes to a separate daughter, where repair or bypass can follow. In the changed lineage the lesion is gone, but its consequence persists.

scenes.tts: Internal chemistry and ordinary copying create spontaneous mutations without an applied mutagen. Outside agents are mutagens when they raise mutation. Both routes end the same way. A change becomes a mutation only if repair or copying leaves a heritable sequence change.
scenes.caption: Internal chemistry and ordinary copying create spontaneous mutations without an applied mutagen. Outside agents are mutagens when they raise mutation. Both routes end the same way. A change becomes a mutation only if repair or copying leaves a heritable sequence change.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the carried conveyor. From the left, a WHITE card labelled 'cell chemistry + copying' (tagged 'spontaneous') sends arrows into BOTH entrances, 'copying error' and 'DNA damage'. From the right, RED cards labelled 'outside agents' (tagged 'induced') also send arrows into BOTH entrances. Both entrances converge on one shared WHITE gate labelled 'heritable sequence change?'. The tags classify the source, not the mechanism.
scenes.narration: Internal chemistry and ordinary copying create spontaneous mutations without an applied mutagen. Outside agents are mutagens when they raise mutation. Both routes end the same way. A change becomes a mutation only if repair or copying leaves a heritable sequence change.

scenes.tts: The effect on a protein may range from none to loss of function, and occasionally a changed or gained function. Those consequences come after the inherited sequence change.
scenes.caption: The effect on a protein may range from none to loss of function, and occasionally a changed or gained function. Those consequences come after the inherited sequence change.
scenes.visual: One yellow-marked strip moves into a neutral output board. Three WHITE branches appear, labelled 'no effect', 'reduced or lost function' and 'changed or gained function (occasional)'; draw the last branch thinner than the other two. Mark the board 'possible outcomes, schematic'. Then fold the branches back into the single yellow sequence block, separating consequence from origin.
scenes.narration: The effect on a protein may range from none to loss of function, and occasionally a changed or gained function. Those consequences come after the inherited sequence change.

scenes.tts: Only after a heritable variant exists can an environment change its representation. The first film followed that later sorting step with phage resistance. Selection cannot reach backward and request that earlier change.
scenes.caption: Only after a heritable variant exists can an environment change its representation. The first film followed that later sorting step with phage resistance. Selection cannot reach backward and request that earlier change.
scenes.visual: The yellow-marked daughter strip zooms back into a yellow bacterial cell. It branches into a small yellow family inside the original culture tube. Only then do RED phage icons appear outside the still-closed gate. A WHITE arrow below the scene reads 'origin first, sorting later' without implying every environment is selective.
scenes.narration: Only after a heritable variant exists can an environment change its representation. The first film followed that later sorting step with phage resistance. Selection cannot reach backward and request that earlier change.

scenes.tts: Damage becomes mutation when repair or copying leaves a heritable sequence change. Repair can erase the damage first. The inherited sequence, not the lesion, is the mutation. A red mark alone never satisfies the definition.
scenes.caption: Damage becomes mutation when repair or copying leaves a heritable sequence change. Repair can erase the damage first. The inherited sequence, not the lesion, is the mutation. A red mark alone never satisfies the definition.
scenes.visual: Return to the large fork. The RED lesion travels down two paths simultaneously. On the GREEN path it disappears into a restored blue strip. On the other, it transforms through copying into a stable YELLOW block shared by descendants. End with the yellow block centred and labelled 'inherited sequence change'.
scenes.narration: Damage becomes mutation when repair or copying leaves a heritable sequence change. Repair can erase the damage first. The inherited sequence, not the lesion, is the mutation. A red mark alone never satisfies the definition.

scenes.tts: The lesson now names the specific sources of these changes. Then the Ames test asks whether a chemical raises mutations in bacteria. Those details belong in the text that follows.
scenes.caption: The lesson now names the specific sources of these changes. Then the Ames test asks whether a chemical raises mutations in bacteria. Those details belong in the text that follows.
scenes.visual: Keep the fork visible. Small blank cards flow toward it under two headings, 'spontaneous sources' and 'induced sources', but do not name any mechanism. At the far right, an unlabeled bacterial plate outline appears with a question mark; show no counts, strains, liver fraction, or answer.
scenes.narration: The lesson now names the specific sources of these changes. Then the Ames test asks whether a chemical raises mutations in bacteria. Those details belong in the text that follows.

scenes.visual: End card over the dimmed moving fork. Show one centred line only, with no subtitle or smaller line: 'Damage becomes mutation when repair or copying leaves a heritable sequence change.'
